title: 1 Kings 15:9–24
context: Asa reigns forty-one years and is judged to have done right, removing idols and even deposing the queen mother Maacah, though the high places remain. Under pressure from Baasha of Israel, he empties the temple treasuries to buy an alliance with Ben Hadad of Syria. Second Chronicles 14-16 gives a longer account, including a prophet’s rebuke of the alliance and differing chronological notes, which are flagged where relevant.

verses.text: In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa began to reign over Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa begins to reign in Jeroboam’s twentieth year. Arminian readers note that a king’s spiritual record is not determined by his father’s, since Asa will choose a very different path.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Asa a work of grace within a compromised dynasty. God raises up reform where the previous reign had failed. His reign shows that a dynasty’s direction can change within one generation.

verses.text: He reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa reigns forty-one years, and his mother is again named Maacah daughter of Abishalom. Arminian readers note that a long reign gives Asa many years of opportunity and responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: The repeated name has led many interpreters to suggest that Maacah was Asa’s grandmother who retained the status of queen mother. Reformed readers treat that as a reasonable proposal rather than a settled fact.

verses.text: Asa did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, as David his father did.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa did what was right in the LORD’s eyes, as David did. Arminian readers see a king who freely chose to honor God, an example of faithful leadership amid a decaying culture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Asa measured by David, the covenant standard. His righteousness is real, though the following verses show it was not without limits. David remains the measuring line for every king of Judah in the book.

verses.text: He put away the sodomites out of the land, and removed all the idols that his fathers had made.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa expels those the WEB calls “sodomites,” a term often understood as cult prostitutes connected with pagan worship (compare 14:24; Deuteronomy 23:17), and removes the idols his fathers made. Arminian readers see decisive personal action against corruption tolerated by earlier kings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see reform aimed at the worship God forbids. Removing idols his own fathers had made required Asa to break with family tradition for the sake of obedience.

verses.text: He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen, because she had made an abominable image for an Asherah. Asa cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa removes Maacah from her position as queen mother because of her Asherah image, and burns it at the Kidron. Arminian readers admire his willingness to put loyalty to God above family ties and court politics.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see reform reaching even the royal household. No relationship is allowed to shelter idolatry, a principle they often connect with Deuteronomy 13:6-10, which warns against following close relatives into false worship.

verses.text: But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect with the LORD all his days.
verses.arminianNotes: The high places were not removed, yet Asa’s heart was wholly true to the LORD all his days. Arminian readers see sincere devotion coexisting with incomplete reform. They take the verdict as encouragement that God honors a sincere heart even where obedience is still incomplete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read perfect here as wholehearted loyalty rather than sinlessness, since later verses record Asa’s failures. Second Chronicles 14:3-5 says Asa removed high places, while 15:17 says they were not removed; many explain this by distinguishing kinds of high places, though the matter is debated.

verses.text: He brought into the LORD’s house the things that his father had dedicated, and the things that he himself had dedicated: silver, gold, and utensils.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa brings dedicated silver, gold, and vessels into the temple. For Arminian readers this is a king honoring his father’s vows and adding his own, an act of grateful devotion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Asa enriches the house of God before the crisis that follows. The treasures he dedicates will soon be taken out again to pay for a foreign alliance.

verses.text: There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.
verses.arminianNotes: War continues between Asa and Baasha all their days. Arminian readers note the constant pressure that tested Asa’s faith and shaped the choices he made.
verses.reformedNotes: Second Chronicles 14:1 and 15:19 speak of periods of peace, and 2 Chronicles 16:1 dates Baasha’s attack to Asa’s thirty-sixth year, later than Baasha’s death according to Kings (16:8). Proposals to reconcile these figures vary, and Reformed readers usually present them as open questions.

verses.text: Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah, and built Ramah, that he might not allow anyone to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha fortifies Ramah to cut off traffic to Judah. Arminian readers see a real threat that called for a response, the kind of crisis in which faith is tested.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the blockade as a test of whether Asa would trust the LORD who had blessed his reforms. The narrator sets up the decision carefully.

verses.text: Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that was left in the treasures of the LORD’s house, and the treasures of the king’s house, and delivered it into the hand of his servants. Then King Asa sent them to Ben Hadad, the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who lived at Damascus, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Asa takes the remaining silver and gold from the temple and palace and sends it to Ben Hadad. Arminian readers see a fateful choice to rely on a foreign king rather than seek the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Second Chronicles 16:7-9 records the seer Hanani rebuking Asa for relying on the king of Syria. Reformed readers see a lapse of faith in an otherwise faithful king, showing that even the godly can stumble.

verses.text: “Let there be a treaty between me and you, like that between my father and your father. Behold, I have sent to you a present of silver and gold. Go, break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, that he may depart from me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Asa asks Ben Hadad to break his treaty with Baasha. Arminian readers note the moral compromise of inducing an ally to betray another agreement. Asa gives away the very treasures he had dedicated to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Asa appeals to an old treaty and a gift of silver rather than to the covenant God. The language of alliance replaces the language of trust.

verses.text: Ben Hadad listened to King Asa, and sent the captains of his armies against the cities of Israel, and struck Ijon, and Dan, and Abel Beth Maacah, and all Chinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali.
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad attacks northern Israel, striking Ijon, Dan, Abel Beth Maacah, and Naphtali. Arminian readers note the human cost of Asa’s strategy for the people of the north.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the plan works militarily, yet success does not prove divine approval. Effective strategy is not the same as faithful obedience. Some interpreters see Syria’s later wars against Israel as growing partly out of this invitation.

verses.text: When Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and lived in Tirzah.
verses.arminianNotes: Baasha stops building Ramah and withdraws to Tirzah. Arminian readers see the immediate relief that made Asa’s alliance seem wise. The withdrawal confirms Asa in a strategy of human alliances rather than prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the short-term gain sets a pattern of reliance on foreign powers that later prophets repeatedly warn against (compare Isaiah 31:1). What looks like deliverance proves to be a costly precedent.

verses.text: Then King Asa made a proclamation to all Judah. No one was exempted. They carried away the stones of Ramah, and its timber, with which Baasha had built; and King Asa used it to build Geba of Benjamin, and Mizpah.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa conscripts all Judah to carry away Ramah’s stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah. Arminian readers note that no one was exempt, a total effort to secure the border.
verses.reformedNotes: Geba and Mizpah were towns in Benjamin’s allotment (Joshua 18:24-26). Reformed readers see the border with Israel fortified in the territory that lay between the two kingdoms.

verses.text: Now the rest of all the acts of Asa, and all his might, and all that he did, and the cities which he built, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah? But in the time of his old age he was diseased in his feet.
verses.arminianNotes: In old age Asa was diseased in his feet. Arminian readers note that the text gives the fact without explanation, and they avoid assuming the illness was a punishment.
verses.reformedNotes: Second Chronicles 16:12 adds that Asa sought physicians rather than the LORD. Reformed readers see a sober reminder that even a faithful king could fail to trust God in his final years.

verses.text: Asa slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in his father David’s city; and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa is buried in David’s city, and Jehoshaphat succeeds him. Arminian readers note a long reign that ended honorably despite its lapses. Kings does not dwell on his failures at the end, letting the overall verdict of 15:11 stand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s continued faithfulness to David’s house, as a godly son follows a largely godly father. Jehoshaphat will receive a similar, largely positive evaluation, continuing the reforming line that Asa began.
